passage.title: Wetlands: nature's sponges
passage.body: A wetland is an area where water covers the soil, or lies near its surface, for all or part of the year. Marshes, mangrove forests and lakes are all wetlands. They slow down flood water and release it gradually, which reduces the damage downstream. Their plants and soil also trap sediments and absorb nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, so the water leaving a wetland is cleaner than the water that entered it. Many migratory birds depend on wetlands for food and rest during their long journeys. Draining wetlands for farming or buildings removes these services. Some wetlands are listed as Ramsar sites, a list of wetlands of international importance.

questions.objective: Find a stated fact in a science passage.
questions.stem: According to the passage, how do wetlands reduce flood damage downstream?
options: They store flood water and release it gradually
They stop rain from falling nearby
They dry up the rivers that feed them
They make water move faster downstream
questions.explanation: The passage says wetlands slow down flood water and release it gradually, which reduces the damage downstream. Storing and slowly releasing the water is exactly this effect.

optionRationale.2: The passage says nothing about wetlands changing rainfall.
optionRationale.3: Wetlands hold water; the passage does not say they dry up rivers.
optionRationale.4: Wetlands slow the flood water down, so it does not move faster.

questions.objective: Identify what a passage does not mention.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as something wetlands do?
options: Providing food and rest for migratory birds
questions.explanation: The passage names three functions: trapping sediments and absorbing nutrients, slowing floods, and supporting migratory birds. It never mentions fossil fuels, so option 4 is the one that is not mentioned.

optionRationale.1: Mentioned: the plants and soil trap sediments.
optionRationale.2: Mentioned: wetlands absorb nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus.
optionRationale.3: Mentioned: many migratory birds depend on wetlands for food and rest.

questions.objective: Draw an inference from a science passage.
questions.stem: If a wetland near a town is drained to build houses, which outcome does the passage suggest?
options: Less flood damage and cleaner water
Loss of flood control, water cleaning and bird habitat
More nutrients absorbed from the water
An increase in the number of Ramsar sites
questions.explanation: The passage says draining wetlands removes their services: slowing flood water, cleaning the water and supporting migratory birds. So the town would lose flood control, water cleaning and bird habitat.

optionRationale.1: This is the opposite of what the passage says about the services that are lost.
optionRationale.3: Draining removes the plants and soil that absorb nutrients, so less is absorbed, not more.
optionRationale.4: The passage gives no link between draining a wetland and the Ramsar list.

questions.objective: Choose the conclusion best supported by a passage.
questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage as a whole?
options: Wetlands are useful to people only when they are turned into farmland
Protecting a wetland also protects services that benefit people and wildlife beyond the wetland itself
Only mangrove forests can make water cleaner
A wetland that is dry for part of the year has no value
questions.explanation: The passage describes services that reach beyond the wetland: reduced damage downstream, cleaner water leaving it, and food and rest for birds on long journeys. Option 2 states this. The other options contradict the passage or claim more than it says.

optionRationale.1: The passage says draining wetlands for farming removes their services.
optionRationale.3: Marshes, lakes and mangroves are all described as wetlands, and plants and soil in wetlands clean water; mangroves are not the only ones.
optionRationale.4: The passage defines a wetland as wet for all or part of the year, so seasonal wetlands still count.

passage.title: Monthly bus passes in a town
passage.body: A town's bus service sold 1,200 monthly passes in January. In February, the number of passes sold rose by 25 per cent. In March, the number sold fell by 20 per cent from the February figure. A pass cost ₹400 in January and February, but the price was raised by ₹50 for March. Every pass sold in a month is paid for in that month at that month's price.

questions.stem: How many passes were sold in February?
questions.explanation: A rise of 25 per cent on 1,200 is 1,200 × 0.25 = 300. So February sales were 1,200 + 300 = 1,500.

optionRationale.1: This adds only 200, which is not 25 per cent of 1,200.
optionRationale.2: This adds 400, which is one third of 1,200, not 25 per cent.
optionRationale.4: This adds 50, which is far less than 25 per cent of 1,200.

questions.stem: How does the number of passes sold in March compare with January?
options: 20 per cent fewer than in January
questions.explanation: February sales were 1,500. A fall of 20 per cent is 1,500 × 0.20 = 300, so March sales were 1,500 − 300 = 1,200. That equals the January figure of 1,200.

optionRationale.1: March sales were 1,200, exactly the January figure, so there is no difference.
optionRationale.2: March sales were 1,200, exactly the January figure, so there is no difference.
optionRationale.3: The 20 per cent fall applies to February's figure, not January's, and the two changes cancel out here.

questions.stem: How much money did the bus service collect from passes in March?
questions.explanation: March sales were 1,200 passes and the March price was ₹400 + ₹50 = ₹450. The collection was 1,200 × 450 = ₹5,40,000.

optionRationale.2: This is 1,200 × ₹400, the old price; the March price was ₹450.
optionRationale.4: This uses a price of ₹425, which is not given in the passage.

questions.objective: Compare totals when quantity and price both change.
questions.stem: By what percentage did the collection from passes change from February to March?
questions.explanation: The February collection was 1,500 × ₹400 = ₹6,00,000 and the March collection was ₹5,40,000. The change is (5,40,000 − 6,00,000) ÷ 6,00,000 = −0.10, a decrease of 10 per cent. The 12.5 per cent price rise only partly offset the 20 per cent fall in sales.

optionRationale.1: This is the fall in the number of passes alone; the higher price softens the fall in money collected.
optionRationale.2: The collections are ₹6,00,000 and ₹5,40,000, which are different.
optionRationale.3: This is the rise in price alone (₹50 on ₹400); the number of passes also fell.

passage.title: Five friends in a row
passage.body: Five friends, Asha, Bala, Chitra, Dev and Esha, sit in a straight row facing north, so that the person at the west end sits furthest to the left of the others. Asha sits at one of the two ends of the row. Bala sits next to Asha. Chitra sits exactly in the middle of the row. Dev does not sit next to Chitra. Esha sits immediately to the right of Chitra.

questions.objective: Place people in a row from clues.
questions.stem: Who sits at the east (right) end of the row?
questions.explanation: Number the seats 1 to 5 from the west end. Chitra is in the middle (seat 3) and Esha is immediately to her right (seat 4). Asha must be at an end and Bala next to her, so Asha is in seat 1 and Bala in seat 2 (seat 5 would leave Bala no free seat next to her). Dev takes seat 5, which is not next to Chitra. The order is Asha, Bala, Chitra, Esha, Dev, so Dev is at the east end.

optionRationale.1: Asha sits in seat 1, at the west end.
optionRationale.2: Bala sits in seat 2, next to Asha.
optionRationale.4: Esha sits in seat 4, immediately to the right of Chitra, not at the end.

questions.objective: Read positions from a completed arrangement.
questions.stem: Who sits between Bala and Esha?
questions.explanation: The order from west to east is Asha, Bala, Chitra, Esha, Dev. Bala is in seat 2 and Esha in seat 4, so only Chitra in seat 3 sits between them.

optionRationale.1: Asha is in seat 1, outside the pair.
optionRationale.3: Dev is in seat 5, outside the pair.
optionRationale.4: Seat 3 lies between seats 2 and 4 and is occupied by Chitra.

questions.stem: How many friends sit to the left (west) of Esha?
questions.explanation: Esha is in seat 4 of the order Asha, Bala, Chitra, Esha, Dev. The seats to her left are 1, 2 and 3, occupied by Asha, Bala and Chitra, so three friends.

optionRationale.2: This leaves out one of Asha, Bala and Chitra.
optionRationale.3: This counts Dev, who sits to the right of Esha.
optionRationale.4: Three friends, not one, sit in seats 1 to 3.

questions.stem: If Bala and Dev exchange seats, who will then sit next to Chitra?
questions.explanation: The original order is Asha, Bala, Chitra, Esha, Dev. After Bala and Dev exchange seats it becomes Asha, Dev, Chitra, Esha, Bala. Chitra is still in seat 3, with Dev on her left and Esha on her right.

optionRationale.1: Bala would move to seat 5, the east end, far from Chitra.
optionRationale.3: Asha stays in seat 1; she is two seats away from Chitra.
optionRationale.4: Esha stays on Chitra's right, and Asha is not next to her.
